title: Comparative Judgement compared with traditional writing assessments
author: Daisy Christodoulou
summary: Christodoulou and Breen use new Australian data to revisit two recurring questions about Comparative Judgement (CJ) writing assessment. They ask whether CJ rewards the same construct as traditional rubric marking, and whether CJ is vulnerable to handwriting bias. Comparing a cohort of 60 Year 5 students' handwritten CJ scores with their typed NAPLAN results, they find a broad correlation and no students with high CJ and low NAPLAN scores. Six outliers scored low on handwritten CJ but higher on typed NAPLAN, and close reading of scripts suggests handwriting difficulty contributed for some, notably funded students in tutoring and Tier 3 instruction. The authors conclude CJ and rubrics broadly measure the same thing and that some students do better typing, while leaving open which format is fairer. The post is an assessment-vendor's own data and should be read as such.
points: On a small cohort, CJ and NAPLAN rubric scores trend together, supporting the claim that both reward the same writing construct.
No student scored high on CJ and low on NAPLAN, while six did the reverse, which points to a handwriting effect rather than a CJ flaw.
Examination of outlier scripts suggests that students who struggle with the physical act of handwriting express themselves better when typing.
The authors argue handwriting bias is more likely in traditional marking, where each script is seen once by one teacher.
The fairness question stays open: typing frees expression, but handwriting still matters for cognitive development and deserves practice and assessment.
quotes: Traditional marking involves the use of a rubric; CJ relies on many educators making many holistic judgements about the quality of different pairs of scripts.

To the extent that the results do disagree, we would say that CJ is often giving the fairer and more valid result, and that rubric-based assessment can end up with distorted results driven by a very rigid tick-box approach.

Because individual CJ decisions are quick, people sometimes worry that teachers may be using shortcuts like handwriting instead. Again, our previous investigations have shown that handwriting bias is much more likely to be an issue with traditional marking, where each script is only ever seen once by one teacher.
As well as the broad correlation, there are no outliers in the bottom right-hand quadrant. This means there are no students getting a high CJ score and a low NAPLAN score.
These students got low scores on the handwritten CJ task, but higher ones on the typed NAPLAN task.
This student struggles with the physical aspect of handwriting, so typing their response may free them up to concentrate on the meaning and mechanics of their writing.

On the other hand, you could say that handwriting still does play a role in life and in cognitive development, and students who struggle with handwriting may benefit from more practice and assessment of it.
